description: The Eatwell Guide, planning balanced meals for different life stages, and catering for specific dietary groups.
content_html:
Guidelines for a Healthy Diet — The Eatwell Guide

The Eatwell Guide is the UK government’s model for a balanced diet. It divides food into five groups and shows roughly what proportion of your plate each should occupy. Because the exam focuses on applying the guide to real meals rather than simply listing percentages, it is worth understanding what each segment means in practice.

  • Fruit and vegetables (roughly one third of the plate) — include fresh, frozen, dried, canned and juiced varieties. At least five 80 g portions per day is the guidance. They supply vitamins, minerals, fibre and antioxidants.
  • Starchy carbohydrates (roughly one third) — bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, oats. Choose wholegrain versions where possible for more fibre and B vitamins.
  • Dairy and dairy alternatives — milk, cheese, yoghurt, and fortified plant milks. Main sources of calcium and iodine.
  • Protein foods — beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and meat alternatives (TVP, tofu, mycoprotein). Eat at least two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily.
  • Oils and spreads — use in small amounts and choose unsaturated options (olive oil, rapeseed oil) rather than butter or lard.

Foods high in fat, salt and sugar — biscuits, cakes, crisps, fizzy drinks — are shown outside the main segments. They are not necessary for a healthy diet and should be eaten less frequently and in small amounts.

Key Fact

The Eatwell Guide has five food groups. Fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates each form roughly one third of the daily plate. Protein foods, dairy and dairy alternatives make up most of the rest. Oils and spreads are used in small amounts. Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the guide.

Portion Size and Costing

When planning a meal, portion size matters for both nutrition and cost. A portion of meat or fish is typically 80–100 g; a portion of cooked pasta or rice is around 180 g. Planning meals in advance, writing a shopping list, using seasonal ingredients, buying own-brand products, and avoiding food waste all reduce the cost of a balanced diet. Costing a recipe means calculating the ingredient cost per serving: divide the cost of the whole pack by the number of portions the pack makes, then add up all the ingredient costs for one serving.

How Nutritional Needs Change Across Life Stages

The body’s needs are not fixed throughout life. Growth, hormone changes, activity levels and the gradual slowing of metabolism all shift what nutrients we need most. The exam lists four life stages to know in detail.

Young Children (1–5 years)

Young children are growing rapidly and need relatively high energy, protein, calcium and vitamin D for bone development. However, their stomachs are small, so meals should be nutritionally dense rather than bulky. Whole (full-fat) milk rather than skimmed milk is recommended up to age 2 because growing toddlers need the fat and fat-soluble vitamins. Salt intake should be kept very low (less than 2 g/day for children aged 1–3). Young children are at higher risk of iron deficiency because they are growing fast; iron-rich foods (red meat, fortified cereals, beans) should be included regularly.

Teenagers

Adolescence brings the biggest growth spurt since infancy. Teenagers have high energy needs, especially if active, and need more protein for muscle development. Calcium and vitamin D are critical: bone density peaks in your early twenties, so what you eat during your teenage years directly affects your risk of osteoporosis decades later. Teenage girls who have started their periods have significantly higher iron needs than boys (because of menstrual blood loss) — and iron-deficiency anaemia is one of the most common nutritional deficiencies in adolescent girls. Folate is also important for all teenagers for healthy cell division.

Adults

Adults have lower energy needs relative to body size than teenagers. The focus shifts to maintaining a healthy body weight, keeping cardiovascular risk low (limiting saturated fat and salt), and eating adequate fibre to reduce the risk of bowel disease and type 2 diabetes. Pregnant and breastfeeding women have additional requirements: folic acid in the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects; iron supports the growing foetus and replaces maternal losses; calcium and vitamin D support fetal bone development; and energy needs increase in the third trimester and during breastfeeding.

The Elderly

Older adults have lower total energy needs because metabolism slows, but their need for protein, calcium, vitamin D and B12 remains high or even increases. Many elderly people have reduced appetite and may be less active, making every mouthful count nutritionally. Vitamin D synthesis in the skin declines with age, and many older adults spend less time outdoors; supplementation is widely recommended. Risk of osteoporosis increases, making calcium intake critical. Dehydration is common in the elderly because the sense of thirst becomes less reliable with age.

Key Fact

Teenage girls need more iron (to replace menstrual losses) and calcium (for peak bone density). Elderly adults need vitamin D (skin synthesis declines), calcium (osteoporosis risk) and vitamin B12 (absorption declines with age) despite lower overall energy needs.

Planning for Specific Dietary Groups

The exam expects you to plan a balanced meal for four specific dietary groups. Each one requires thought about nutrient gaps and practical substitutions.

A vegetarian diet excludes meat and fish. A vegan diet excludes all animal products. Both must plan carefully to avoid deficiencies. Key nutrients at risk in vegan diets: vitamin B12 (only in animal foods or fortified products), vitamin D (few dietary plant sources), calcium (dairy is the main UK source — must use fortified plant milks or eat plenty of kale and tofu), iron (non-haem iron from plant foods is less well absorbed — eat with vitamin C), omega-3 fats (oily fish is absent — flaxseed, walnuts, algae-based supplements). Protein: use complementation and soya/tofu/mycoprotein.

Coeliac disease requires a strict gluten-free diet. Gluten is found in wheat, barley and rye — so ordinary bread, pasta, biscuits and cakes are off-limits. Substitutes include rice, maize (corn), potatoes, gluten-free oats, and purpose-made gluten-free products. Cross-contamination in the kitchen must be prevented. Lactose intolerance means the person cannot digest lactose, the sugar in cow’s milk, due to insufficient lactase enzyme. Symptoms include bloating and diarrhoea. Alternatives: lactose-free milk, hard cheeses (lower in lactose), small amounts of yoghurt (fermentation reduces lactose), and calcium-fortified plant milks. A high-fibre diet benefits people at risk of constipation, bowel disease or type 2 diabetes. It should include wholegrain bread and cereals, plenty of vegetables and pulses, and fruit.

Maintaining a Healthy Body Weight

A healthy body weight is maintained when energy intake equals energy expenditure — this is called energy balance. Regular physical activity, eating plenty of fibre (which promotes satiety), limiting high-fat and high-sugar foods, and eating regular meals (which prevents extreme hunger leading to overeating) all support a healthy weight throughout life. Making informed food choices means reading labels, understanding portion sizes, and choosing cooking methods that add less fat (grilling rather than frying, baking rather than deep-frying).
exam_tip_html: Questions about specific dietary groups or life stages nearly always use the command word Explain or Evaluate. Remember: Explain means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — so link the dietary need to the biological reason and the practical food choice. For example: “A teenage girl needs more iron because menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores, which means she should eat red meat, fortified cereals or lentils alongside a source of vitamin C to maximise absorption.” Avoid writing only that a person “needs to eat healthily” or “should have a balanced diet” — these are too vague to earn marks. Name specific nutrients, specific foods, and specific reasons.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Eatwell Guide shows a balanced diet: roughly one third fruit and vegetables, one third starchy carbohydrates, with protein foods, dairy and small amounts of unsaturated fats. Foods high in fat, salt and sugar are outside the guide.
  • Nutritional needs change with life stage. Young children and teenagers need high calcium and vitamin D for bone development; teenage girls need extra iron; the elderly need vitamin D, calcium and B12 despite lower energy needs.
  • Vegetarians and vegans must plan for B12, vitamin D, calcium and iron. People with coeliac disease must avoid gluten; those with lactose intolerance need dairy alternatives. A high-fibre diet supports gut health and reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes and bowel disease.

practice_questions.text: Name the five food groups shown in the Eatwell Guide.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all five named correctly: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; dairy and dairy alternatives; protein foods (beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and alternatives); oils and spreads. Accept a clearly correct description of any five distinct groups. (1 mark for all five; do not award for a partial list of fewer than four.)

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why teenage girls may have higher iron requirements than boys of the same age.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores each month; rapid growth during adolescence increases the demand for iron (for haemoglobin and muscle development); teenage girls are sometimes more likely to have restricted diets that are low in red meat. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three adaptations a cook should make when preparing a three-course meal for a guest with coeliac disease.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct, relevant points: replace wheat-based pasta/bread/flour with gluten-free alternatives (rice, gluten-free pasta, gluten-free flour); ensure all equipment and surfaces have been thoroughly cleaned to prevent cross-contamination from gluten-containing foods; check all processed ingredients (sauces, stocks, dressings) for hidden gluten; use gluten-free bread or gluten-free crackers for any starter; choose desserts based on rice, potato starch or gluten-free oats rather than wheat-based pastry or sponge. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Oliver is 70 years old, lives alone, and rarely goes outdoors. His doctor has suggested his vitamin D levels may be low. Explain why Oliver is at risk and identify two steps he could take to improve his vitamin D status.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed point. (1) Risk: vitamin D is synthesised in the skin when it is exposed to sunlight; because Oliver rarely goes outdoors, his skin synthesis will be minimal. This is compounded by the fact that ageing reduces the skin's ability to synthesise vitamin D. Without adequate vitamin D, calcium absorption is impaired, risking bone loss and osteomalacia. (2) Steps: take a vitamin D supplement (Public Health England recommends 10 micrograms per day for all adults, especially those over 65); eat vitamin-D-rich foods such as oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), eggs and fortified cereals or spreads. 1 mark for identifying the mechanism of risk; 1 mark for developed consequence, per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways that planning meals in advance can help a family on a limited budget to eat a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: writing a shopping list prevents impulse purchases and reduces overspending; planning uses up all ingredients and reduces food waste; buying seasonal ingredients (e.g. root vegetables in winter) is cheaper; batch cooking and freezing reduces the cost per portion; choosing own-brand or supermarket-own versions of staples (pasta, tinned tomatoes, oats) without reducing nutritional quality. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: A school canteen is redesigning its menu to better support the nutritional needs of 11- to 16-year-old students. Evaluate the extent to which the canteen should prioritise calcium and vitamin D in its menu planning, using your knowledge of the nutritional needs of this age group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Argues both sides with evidence. FOR prioritising calcium and vitamin D: bone density peaks in the early twenties, so the teenage years are a critical window; calcium is needed for bone mineralisation and muscle function; vitamin D is needed for calcium absorption; deficiency during adolescence increases osteoporosis risk in later life; many teenagers eat too little dairy (fear of fat) or have inadequate sun exposure; calcium-rich foods (dairy, fortified plant milks, dark green vegetables) are affordable and easy to include. AGAINST/nuancing: a school canteen cannot address home eating; teenagers also have high needs for iron (especially girls), protein, folate and iodine; a menu solely focused on calcium and vitamin D may neglect variety; individual variation means some students (vegans, lactose intolerant) cannot benefit from dairy-based sources unless alternatives are offered. JUDGEMENT: explicitly stated and supported (e.g. 'Calcium and vitamin D should be a priority, but the canteen should simultaneously address iron for girls and protein variety — a menu-planning checklist rather than a single-nutrient focus would be most effective.'). Accurate use of vitamin D, calcium, peak bone density, osteoporosis, haemoglobin, RNI terminology throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Addresses both calcium/vitamin D case AND at least one other competing nutritional priority. Reaches a judgement but the weighing may be partial or the evidence one-sided.

Developing (4–6 marks): Describes calcium and/or vitamin D needs without sustained analysis of both sides; may list foods without explaining the reasoning; judgement weak or absent.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about teenagers needing calcium with little or no development, application to the canteen context, or judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: According to current healthy-eating guidelines, which two food groups should together make up roughly two thirds of the daily diet?
options: Fruit and vegetables, and starchy carbohydrates
Oils and spreads, and protein foods

knowledge_checks.q: A lacto-ovo vegetarian would eat which of the following?
options: Meat and fish but no dairy
Dairy and eggs but no meat or fish
Fish but no meat or dairy

knowledge_checks.q: People with _____ disease must follow a strict gluten-free diet because gluten triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine.
Elderly adults have lower total energy needs than younger adults, but their requirement for vitamin D, _____ and B12 remains high or increases.
Match each life stage with its most distinctive nutritional priority.
right: High calcium and vitamin D for bone development; full-fat milk recommended under 2
Higher iron intake to replace menstrual losses and support rapid growth
Vitamin D supplement recommended; calcium for osteoporosis prevention

flashcard_questions.q: How many of the five food groups does the Eatwell Guide recommend form roughly two thirds of daily intake?
flashcard_questions.a: Two groups — fruit and vegetables, and starchy carbohydrates.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is full-fat milk recommended for children under 2 rather than skimmed milk?
flashcard_questions.a: Growing toddlers need the fat and fat-soluble vitamins A and D for development.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do teenage girls have higher iron needs than teenage boys?
flashcard_questions.a: Menstrual blood loss each month depletes iron stores that must be replaced.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the peak bone density window and why does it matter for teenagers?
flashcard_questions.a: Bone density peaks in the early twenties; adequate calcium during teenage years reduces osteoporosis risk in later life.

flashcard_questions.q: What nutrient is almost absent from non-fortified plant foods, making it a key concern for vegans?

flashcard_questions.a: An autoimmune condition where gluten triggers immune damage to the small intestine lining.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two gluten-free alternatives to wheat-based pasta.
Why does lactose intolerance cause digestive symptoms after drinking cow's milk?
flashcard_questions.a: Insufficient lactase enzyme means lactose is not digested and ferments in the gut.
When daily energy intake equals daily energy expenditure, maintaining a stable body weight.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is vitamin C helpful when eating iron-rich plant foods?
flashcard_questions.a: It converts non-haem iron into a form the body absorbs more easily.

glossary_terms.definition: The UK government's visual guide showing the proportions of the five food groups that together make up a healthy, balanced diet.
A person who does not eat meat or fish but may eat eggs and dairy products.
A person who eats no animal products at all, including no meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey.
An autoimmune condition in which gluten triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine.
An inability to fully digest lactose (the sugar in milk) due to insufficient lactase enzyme, causing bloating and digestive discomfort.
